faq.a: Low protein intake or muscle wasting reduces urea generation, so toxin accumulation may be present despite a normal level.
faq.q: Why can a patient with normal urea still have uraemia?

faq.a: Percussion over the left lower chest reveals a dullness that shifts with position; a friction rub on auscultation confirms pericardial inflammation.
faq.q: What is the first bedside test for uraemic pericarditis?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with malaria presents with oliguria, K⁺ = 6.8 mmol/L and ECG peaked T waves – what is the immediate management and why? — Immediate calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and arrange emergency dialysis; prevents fatal arrhythmia.
How does uraemic pericarditis differ clinically from bacterial pericarditis? — Uraemic pericarditis lacks fever, shows a friction rub, and improves with dialysis rather than antibiotics.

A patient on chronic haemodialysis develops pruritus and nausea; labs show urea 30 mmol/L, creatinine 900 µmol/L. What does this indicate and what is the next step? — Persistent uraemic symptoms despite dialysis suggest inadequate clearance; increase dialysis dose or frequency.
Explain why loop diuretics are ineffective in anuric patients with uraemia. — No urine output means diuretics cannot promote natriuresis; dialysis is required to remove fluid and toxins.

What investigations would you order if ultrasound is unavailable but you suspect obstructive uraemia? — Serum electrolytes, renal function, urinalysis for obstruction clues, and a plain abdominal X‑ray to look for hydronephrosis signs.

Distinguish between acute tubular necrosis and acute interstitial nephritis as causes of uraemia in a patient with recent herbal remedy use. — ATN shows muddy brown casts, often ischemic; AIN shows eosinophils, rash, and recent drug exposure; both raise creatinine but management differs.
Why is ACE‑I/ARB use cautioned in advanced uraemia, and when is it still beneficial? — They can raise potassium and reduce GFR, but they slow CKD progression when potassium is controlled.

A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with flank pain and rising creatinine; what uraemic complications should you anticipate? — Risk of papillary necrosis, haematuria, and rapid progression to acute kidney injury; monitor for hyperkalaemia and need for dialysis.
ai.title: Uraemia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Uraemia is the clinical syndrome of toxin accumulation due to severe renal failure. It requires prompt recognition, staging, identification of reversible causes and urgent dialysis when life‑threatening features appear.

b: Diagnosed by elevated serum urea (>20 mmol/L) and creatinine (>500 µmol/L) plus clinical features.
sections.p: Uraemia denotes the systemic effects of retained nitrogenous waste (urea, creatinine, guanidines) when glomerular filtration rate (GFR) falls below ~10 mL/min/1.73 m².

b: Stage 5 CKD: GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m², often asymptomatic until toxin load rises.
Uraemic emergency: refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis, pericarditis, encephalopathy, or uncontrolled fluid overload.
sections.p: Kidney disease is staged by GFR; uraemic syndrome usually appears in stage 5 (GFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m²).

b: Severe dehydration from diarrhoea or malaria.
Obstructive uropathy (prostate hypertrophy, stones, schistosomal fibrosis).
Acute tubular necrosis from sepsis, severe malaria, or nephrotoxic herbal remedies.
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (post‑streptococcal, lupus, HIV‑associated).
Chronic kidney disease from hypertension, diabetes, sickle‑cell nephropathy.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the common precipitants of acute uraemia are:

b: Neurological: lethargy, confusion, asterixis, seizures, uraemic encephalopathy.
Cardiovascular: pericardial friction rub, hypotension, arrhythmias from hyperkalaemia.
Gastro‑intestinal: nausea, vomiting, anorexia, pruritus, gastrointestinal bleeding.
Dermatological: pallor, uremic frost, pruritic excoriations.
Respiratory: rapid shallow breathing if metabolic acidosis dominates.
sections.p: Uraemia produces multisystem signs that reflect toxin accumulation and fluid/electrolyte imbalance.

t.b: Quantifies renal clearance loss; values >20 mmol/L urea or >500 µmol/L creatinine support uraemia.

t.a: Estimated GFR (eGFR) using CKD‑EPI or MDRD
t.b: Staging of CKD; <15 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates stage 5.
Detects hyperkalaemia (>6 mmol/L) or severe acidosis (HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L).
Assesses metabolic acidosis; pH < 7.30 with HCO₃⁻ <15 mmol/L signals urgent dialysis.
Helps identify obstructive or glomerular causes; presence of casts, protein, or haematuria guides further work‑up.
Detects obstruction, kidney size, and echogenicity; if unavailable, rely on clinical signs of obstruction.
Looks for pulmonary oedema or pericardial calcification when cardiac involvement suspected.

b: Refractory hyperkalaemia (>6 mmol/L) with ECG changes.
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.30).
Uraemic pericarditis with tamponade signs.
Encephalopathy causing decreased consciousness.
Pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics.
sections.p: Complications that demand immediate action include:

b: Fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline if hypovolaemic; avoid overload.
Loop diuretic (furosemide) when urine output >200 mL/day and potassium is high.
Emergency haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis for: hyperkalaemia >6 mmol/L, pH < 7.30, pericarditis, refractory fluid overload, severe nausea/vomiting.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, certain herbal preparations).
Correct electrolyte disturbances: calcium gluconate for cardiac protection in hyperkalaemia, insulin/glucose to shift K⁺ intracellularly.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, remove excess fluid/toxins, and provide renal replacement when indicated.

b: Regular monitoring of eGFR, electrolytes, blood pressure.
Control hypertension (ACE‑I/ARB) and diabetes (metformin avoided if eGFR < 30).
Vaccinations (HBV, pneumococcal, influenza).
Education on avoiding nephrotoxins and proper hydration.
sections.p: After acute stabilization, long‑term care focuses on slowing CKD progression and preparing for chronic dialysis or transplantation.

b: Severe hepatic encephalopathy – distinguished by elevated bilirubin, coagulopathy, and absent renal failure.
Sepsis‑related encephalopathy – usually accompanied by high white cell count and source of infection.
Hyperthyroidism crisis – tachycardia and weight loss predominate, thyroid labs are abnormal.
Serum urea may be normal in low‑protein diets despite severe GFR loss.
Creatinine can be falsely low in muscle‑wasting patients (e.g., advanced HIV or malnutrition).
Potassium may appear normal if intracellular shift occurs; always check ECG.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness, seizures, or severe confusion.
Chest pain with pericardial rub or signs of tamponade.
Rapidly rising potassium >6 mmol/L or ECG changes.
Severe dyspnoea with pulmonary oedema unresponsive to diuretics.
